characters: A grandmother and a grandchild talking in a kitchen, a river, a band of drummers of different ages, and a seed being planted.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, proud voice with a steady rhythm, slowing on the last line of each stanza
narrationPlan.pace: Warm and steady, building pride towards the end (about 80 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Gentle strings and soft hand percussion (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Ghana has many languages. The poem does not name any one language so that every child can hear their own mother tongue in it. It mentions English and French because English is the official language and French is spoken in neighbouring countries.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the rhyme pairs in each stanza (wide/side, knew/through; land/band, own/known; ground/sound, skies/rise; true/anew, soil/toil) are accepted rhymes in Ghanaian English.
Check the metre is natural to read aloud.

teacherGuide.overview: A rhymed poem that practises the BECE vocabulary of form and figures of speech. Form: four quatrains (four-line stanzas) with rhyme scheme ABAB in each. Devices: metaphor (river, drum), simile (like a drum, like seed to the soil), imagery, alliteration (safe and sound), contrast (English and French versus mother tongue). Theme: pride in one’s mother tongue. Tone: warm and proud.
learningGoals: Find a metaphor, a simile and alliteration.
State the theme and tone in a sentence.
beforeReading: Ask: which proverb do you know in your mother tongue?
whileReading: At each stanza, ask learners to underline the last word of every line and label A or B.
afterReading: Write a four-line stanza in ABAB about your mother tongue.
Make a chart: device, example, effect.
discussion: Why does the poet compare a language to a river and a drum?
What is the poet’s attitude to English and French?
reflection: What would be lost if a language disappeared?

support: Provide a sheet with the poem and blanks for the rhyme letters.
stretch: Compare this poem’s theme with another poem on identity.

culturalNotes: Ghana has many languages. The poem does not name any one language so that every child can hear their own mother tongue in it. It mentions English and French because English is the official language and French is spoken in neighbouring countries.
localiseThis: Invite elders or older learners to say a proverb in your local language and translate it.
Do not rank languages; value every learner’s mother tongue.
